title: The Word Became Flesh; the First Disciples
summary: John opens with a prologue about the Word who was with God and was God in the beginning, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth. John the Baptist then testifies that he is not the Christ but a voice preparing the way, and he points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Andrew, Simon Peter, Philip, and Nathanael begin to follow Jesus, who promises that they will see heaven opened.
story: Matthew begins with Abraham, Mark with John the Baptist, and Luke with the birth of John and Jesus. John begins before the world. His first words, “In the beginning”, repeat the first words of Genesis, and he tells us that the one about to walk onto the stage of history was there when the curtain first rose, as the Word through whom God made everything. The prologue (verses 1 to 18) gives the reader, in advance, the knowledge the characters in the story lack. Then the narrative starts, and day by day (verses 29, 35, 43) one witness after another names who Jesus is: Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses wrote about, King of Israel, Son of Man. The whole Gospel will unfold these titles.
historical:
John the Baptist was a well-known prophetic figure who preached repentance and baptized in the Jordan. Josephus, the Jewish historian writing in the 90s AD, describes him as a good man who called Jews to righteousness and baptism and was executed by Herod Antipas. His movement continued after his death (Acts 19:1-7 finds disciples of John at Ephesus), which may be one reason the Gospel stresses so firmly that he was not the Light but a witness to it. The delegation of priests and Levites from Jerusalem, and later Pharisees, reflects the authorities' concern with any figure who drew crowds in the wilderness, a place associated with a new exodus and with messianic hopes.

Bethany beyond the Jordan is a different place from the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived, and its exact location is uncertain. Bethsaida, home of Andrew, Peter, and Philip, lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee. Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the Galilean hills, not mentioned in the Old Testament, which helps explain Nathanael's scorn.
cultural:
Jewish expectation in the period included several figures. The Christ or Messiah (both mean anointed one) was the hoped-for king from David's line. Elijah was expected to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). The Prophet recalled Moses' promise that God would raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15). John denies being any of them. Untying sandals was a menial task, sometimes assigned to slaves, and some later Jewish sources say a disciple should serve his teacher in everything except this, which gives force to John's words that he is not worthy even of that.

The word logos, translated Word, had meanings for both Jewish and Greek readers. For Jewish readers it recalled God's creative word in Genesis 1 (and God said), his word that came to the prophets, and the figure of Wisdom who was with God at creation in Proverbs 8. Some Jewish writers, especially Philo of Alexandria, had already used logos for God's agency in the world. For Greek readers, especially those influenced by Stoic philosophy, logos named the rational principle ordering the universe. John's prologue speaks to both worlds and then says what neither expected: the Word became flesh. The tenth hour, when the first disciples went with Jesus, was about four in the afternoon, counting from sunrise.
literary: The prologue is carefully composed prose with a poetic rhythm, and many scholars think it is built on or shaped like a hymn. Key words pass from line to line like a chain: Word, God, life, light, darkness. It moves from the Word with God in eternity (verses 1 to 5), to the witness of John (verses 6 to 8), to the Light coming into a world that did not receive him (verses 9 to 13), to the Word made flesh and the Son who makes the Father known (verses 14 to 18). Some see a chiastic shape, with verse 12 (the right to become children of God) at its center. After the prologue the chapter becomes narrative, arranged over successive days, and a pattern appears that recurs throughout the Gospel: one person finds Jesus and brings another, and the invitation “Come and see” is repeated (verses 39 and 46).

outline.t: The Word in the beginning: life and light
John, a witness to the Light
John's testimony: not the Christ, but a voice
Andrew and Simon Peter follow Jesus

doctrines.note: The Word was with God and was God: distinct from the Father, yet sharing his divine nature. Verse 18 calls the Son “Himself God” at the Father's side (the best early manuscripts read one and only God, while others read one and only Son), and verses 32 and 33 show the Spirit descending and resting on him. The church's later doctrine of the Trinity is built largely from texts like these.

Jesus is the Word made flesh: truly God and truly human. The incarnation does not mean God pretended to be human or that a human was promoted to divinity. The eternal Word took human nature, and in Jesus God's glory was seen.

“Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.” John places the Son at the work of creation, echoing Genesis 1. The one who redeems the world is the one who made it.

John the Baptist calls Jesus “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” The image gathers several Old Testament strands: the Passover lamb, the daily sacrificial lambs, and the servant of Isaiah 53 led like a lamb to slaughter. His death will deal with sin itself, for the whole world.

words.note: Logos, word. In ordinary Greek it means a spoken word, a message, a reason, or an account. John uses it as a title for the eternal Son, who expresses God as a word expresses the speaker's mind. Jewish readers would think of God creating by his word and sending his word through the prophets; Greek readers of the reason that orders the world. John claims both and surpasses both: this Word is a person, and he became flesh.

Skēnoō, to pitch a tent, to dwell. The Word made His dwelling among us, literally tented or tabernacled among us. The verb recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness, where God's glory filled the tent (Exodus 40:34). John says that the glory which once filled the tabernacle has now been seen in the flesh of Jesus.

Monogenēs, one and only, unique. Older translations rendered it only begotten, linking it to birth; most scholars now think it means unique, one of a kind, though it is used for an only child. Jesus is the Son in a sense no one else is, even though believers become children of God (verse 12).

Exēgeomai, to make known, to explain, to lead out. The Son has made the Father known. English exegesis comes from this word. No one has seen God, but Jesus is his exegesis, the full explanation of who God is.

christ: Few chapters in the Bible say more about who Jesus is. He existed before creation, was with God and was God, and made all things. He is the life and light of humanity. He became flesh, a full human being, and dwelt among us, revealing the glory of God, full of grace and truth, the very words Exodus 34:6 uses of God himself (abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness). He is greater than Moses: the law came through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. He is the Lamb who takes away sin, the one on whom the Spirit rests, the Messiah, the Son of God, and the King of Israel. His final promise alludes to Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28:12), where angels went up and down a ladder between heaven and earth. Jesus says the angels will ascend and descend on the Son of Man: he is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel, the house of God.

hard.q: Some translations read that the Word was a god. What does John 1:1 actually say?
hard.a: The Greek of the last clause places the word God first and has no article before it, literally God was the Word. Jehovah's Witnesses, in their New World Translation, render it the Word was a god, arguing that the lack of an article makes the noun indefinite. Almost all Greek scholars, of every theological persuasion, reject that reading. In Greek a noun placed before the verb without an article often describes quality or nature rather than identity, so the clause means that the Word had the full nature of God, what God was the Word was, without saying that the Word is the same person as the Father (who is the God the Word was with, in the previous clause). John uses God without the article elsewhere in the same chapter to refer to the one true God (verses 6, 12, 13, and 18), so the absence of the article cannot mean a lesser deity. The verse holds together what the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity: the Word is distinct from the Father and fully divine. John's monotheism is Jewish and uncompromising, and in that world there is no category for a second, lesser god.

questions: John says the Word became flesh. What difference does it make that God came in a human body rather than only sending a message?
Andrew brought his brother and Philip told Nathanael, “Come and see.” Who first brought you to Jesus, or whom might you invite?
Nathanael's first reaction was prejudice about where Jesus came from. What assumptions might keep you from seeing where God is at work?
